items.title: 11.4.2 Graph of y = sin x from - 2pi to 2pi

source_refs.note: Book p. 206-207: 11.4.2 Graph of y = sin x: range lines y = +/-1, table x / sin x, 'To draw the graph' steps (i)-(iv), Note box, graphs 0 to 360 and -360 to 360, 'cycle', properties (i)-(xi).

blocks.text: We know that the period of sine function is \(2\pi\), so we will first draw the graph for the interval from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) (from \(0\) to \(2\pi\)).

To graph the sine function, first, recall that \(-1 \le \sin x \le 1\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). We know the range of the sine function is \([-1, 1]\), so the graph will be between the horizontal lines \(y = +1\) and \(y = -1\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Two facts make the work short. Period \(2\pi\): after \(360^{\circ}\) the values repeat, so one interval of length \(2\pi\) shows everything; the rest of the graph is copies of it. Range \([-1, 1]\): the curve never goes above \(y = 1\) or below \(y = -1\), so we draw these two lines first (dashed) as a frame.
The table of the ordered pairs satisfying \(y = \sin x\) is as follows:

blocks.caption: Ordered pairs satisfying \(y = \sin x\), \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\) (printed across the page in the book; turned on its side here to fit a phone)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where do the values come from? \(\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.87\) and \(\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5\). The others use the identities of 11.4, e.g. \(\sin 150^{\circ} = \sin(180^{\circ} - 30^{\circ}) = 0.5\) and \(\sin 240^{\circ} = \sin(180^{\circ} + 60^{\circ}) = -0.87\). Notice the pattern: from \(180^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) the values are those of \(0^{\circ}\) to \(180^{\circ}\) with a minus sign, because \(\sin(\pi + \theta) = -\sin\theta\).

items: (i) Take a convenient scale: 1 side of small square on the \(x\)-axis \(= 10^{\circ}\); 1 side of big square on the \(y\)-axis \(= 1\) unit.
(iii) Plot the points corresponding to the ordered pairs in the table above, i.e., \((0, 0)\), \((30^{\circ}, 0.5)\), \((60^{\circ}, 0.87)\) and so on.
(iv) Join the points with the help of a smooth curve as shown. So, we get the graph of \(y = \sin x\) from \(0\) to \(360^{\circ}\), i.e., from \(0\) to \(2\pi\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The graphs of trigonometric functions are smooth curves: none of them is made of line segments, and none has sharp corners or breaks within its domain. This behaviour of the curve is called continuity; it means that the trigonometric functions are continuous wherever they are defined. Moreover, as the trigonometric functions are periodic, their curves repeat after fixed intervals.

blocks.alt: Graph of y = sin x from 0 to 360 degrees. Magenta axes; the x-axis is marked every 30 degrees, the y-axis has small ticks every 0.1 and labels 1, .5, minus .5, minus 1. Dashed lines y = 1 and y = minus 1. The table points (except the zeros at 0, 180 and 360 degrees) are dots on one smooth wave: up from (0, 0) to the maximum (90, 1), down through (180, 0) to the minimum (270, minus 1), and back to (360, 0).
blocks.caption: Graph of y = sin x from 0° to 360° (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Read the shape in four quarters: from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(90^{\circ}\) the curve rises from \(0\) to \(1\); from \(90^{\circ}\) to \(180^{\circ}\) it falls back to \(0\); from \(180^{\circ}\) to \(270^{\circ}\) it falls to \(-1\); from \(270^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) it rises back to \(0\). The curve is positive in Quadrants I and II and negative in Quadrants III and IV, exactly as the signs of sine in those quadrants.

In the similar way, we can draw the graph for the interval from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(-360^{\circ}\). This will complete the graph of \(y = \sin x\) from \(-360^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\) (from \(-2\pi\) to \(2\pi\)), which is given below:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: For negative angles use \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\): \(\sin(-30^{\circ}) = -0.5\), \(\sin(-90^{\circ}) = -1\), \(\sin(-270^{\circ}) = 1\). So the left half of the graph is the right half turned through half a turn about the origin.

blocks.alt: Graph of y = sin x from minus 360 to 360 degrees, x-axis marked every 30 degrees, y labels 1, .5, minus .5, minus 1. Two complete waves between the dashed lines y = 1 and y = minus 1: maxima at minus 270 and 90 degrees, minima at minus 90 and 270 degrees, zeros at minus 360, minus 180, 0, 180 and 360 degrees. Dots at the 30-degree points that are not multiples of 90 degrees. The curve passes through the origin.
blocks.caption: Graph of y = sin x from −360° to 360° (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: The graph in the interval \([0, 2\pi]\) is called a cycle. Since the period of sine function is \(2\pi\), the sine graph can be extended on both sides of the \(x\)-axis through every interval of \(2\pi\).
Properties of graph of sine function (y = sin x)

items: (i) The domain is the set of real numbers \((-\infty < x < \infty)\).
(ii) The range includes all real numbers from \(-1\) to \(1\), inclusive, \([-1, 1]\).
(iii) The graph of sine function is continuous for all real numbers.
(iv) The period of sine function is \(2\pi\). Mathematically, we can express it as \(\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin\theta\).
(v) The sine function is an odd function. As the graph of sine function is symmetric about the origin. Mathematically, it can be written as \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\).
(vi) The maximum value of \(y = \sin x\) is \(1\) when \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi n\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(vii) The minimum value of \(y = \sin x\) is \(-1\) when \(x = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2\pi n\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(viii) The \(x\)-intercept of the sine function occurs at \(x = \pi n\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(ix) The \(y\)-intercept of the sine function is \(0\).
(x) The amplitude of sine function is \(1\).
(xi) In unit circle \(\sin\theta\) is equal to the \(y\)-coordinate of the given point.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Check the properties on the graph. (vi) with \(n = 0\) gives \(x = 90^{\circ}\) and with \(n = -1\) gives \(x = -270^{\circ}\): both are peaks in the figure. (viii) with \(n = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2\) gives \(-360^{\circ}, -180^{\circ}, 0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}\): exactly where the curve cuts the \(x\)-axis. (x) amplitude \(1\) is the height of a peak above the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When asked for the maximum or minimum of \(\sin x\), give both the value and where it occurs: maximum \(1\) at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\); minimum \(-1\) at \(x = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Draw one cycle (\(0\) to \(2\pi\)) from the table, then repeat it every \(2\pi\).
2. The curve stays between \(y = -1\) and \(y = 1\) and passes through the origin.
3. Zeros at \(n\pi\), peaks at \(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\), lowest points at \(\frac{3\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\).
4. Odd function: the graph is symmetric about the origin.
5. A smooth, continuous wave: no corners, no breaks.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Drawing pointed peaks at \(90^{\circ}\) and \(270^{\circ}\): the top and bottom of the wave are rounded.
2. Starting the sine graph at \((0, 1)\): that is cosine. Sine starts at the origin.
3. Writing the period as \(\pi\): one full up-and-down wave takes \(2\pi\).
